meta.title: Saved, refreshed, reverted: replica lag
meta.story: A profile service writes to a Postgres primary and serves reads from two streaming replicas. It has worked for years. This afternoon a user renames herself, gets a green 'Saved', hits refresh, and her old name is back.

background.title: The system
background.body: profile-api serves a consumer app. Every write goes to one Postgres primary. Reads, the large majority of traffic, go to two streaming replicas, which keeps the primary free for writes.

background.title: How it normally works
background.body: The primary records every change in its write-ahead log (WAL) and streams it to each replica, which replays it in order. A replica is usually a few milliseconds behind, so nobody notices that a read can come from the slightly-past.

background.title: Today
background.body: The data team starts a backfill that rewrites a column on 42 million user rows. A few seconds later, Maya renames herself and refreshes the page.

dashboard.title: Replica replay lag
dashboard.why: How far a replica is behind the primary. Anything a user reads from a lagging replica can be stale.

dashboard.title: WAL: generated vs replayed
dashboard.why: The primary writes WAL; each replica must replay it. When generated outruns replayed, a backlog builds.

dashboard.title: Reads that miss your own write
dashboard.why: The user-visible symptom: a read right after your own write returns the old value.

dashboard.title: Reads served by primary
dashboard.why: The cost of the fix: reads pinned to the primary add load to the one server that takes all writes.

dashboard.title: Backfill rows / s
dashboard.why: The trigger. The backfill's speed sets how much WAL the primary produces.

dashboard.title: Replica CPU (4 cores)
dashboard.why: Rules out the obvious wrong fix: replicas are not busy, so more hardware would not help.

dashboard.title: Primary CPU
dashboard.why: Shows what the backfill and the pinned reads cost the primary.

dashboard.title: profile-api p99
dashboard.why: What users feel on the API. Reads moved to the primary get a bit slower.

dashboard.title: Support tickets / 5 min
dashboard.why: The business signal. Support tickets are often the first alarm for stale reads.

dashboard.title: WAL on disk (replica-2)
dashboard.why: The backlog itself: WAL the replica has received but not yet replayed.

beat.hint: Writes go to pg-primary. Reads go to two replicas that replay the primary's WAL (its change log) over async streaming replication. Replay lag is about 30ms, so a read right after a write almost always sees it.

notes.text: Replay lag ~30ms: replicas are effectively current
Replicas replay WAL as fast as the primary writes it

feed.text: kicking off the users.tz backfill now, 42M rows in 50k batches. should be done by EOD
UPDATE users SET tz = … WHERE id BETWEEN $1 AND $1+50000 (no pause between batches)
PATCH /v1/profile user=4812 display_name='Maya R.' → pg-primary 200 (7ms) commit_lsn=3A/1F00C2D8
ticket #88213: 'changed my name, it said saved, refreshed 3 times and it's back to the old one'

beat.hint: The write committed on the primary and returned 200. But the refresh was routed to pg-replica-2, which had only replayed WAL up to 3A/1C9E…, before Maya's commit at 3A/1F00…. Nothing is broken: async replicas are allowed to be behind.

notes.text: Reads right after a write now return the old row
Replica ~8s behind: any read inside that window is stale

feed.text: replica lag 13s and climbing, replica CPU is only 30%. add a third replica to spread the reads?
LOG: startup process (PID 812) recovering 000000010000003A000000F4; wal_receiver 2.1 GB ahead

beat.hint: The backfill makes the primary write 70 MB/s of WAL. Each replica replays it in one startup process, topping out near 50 MB/s, so lag grows ~0.3s every second. A third replica would replay the same WAL just as slowly: it adds read capacity, not freshness.

notes.text: Replay held flat at its ~50 MB/s ceiling; 70 MB/s arrives
Lag grows at the gap: ~0.3s per second

feed.text: two fixes: app reads its own writes from primary, and Priya throttles the backfill
profile-api v2.14: after a write, store commit LSN in session; read from primary until replica replay_lsn ≥ it

beat.hint: Lag is still ~28s, yet nobody sees their old name. A user who just wrote reads from the primary until a replica has replayed past their commit LSN (pg_last_wal_replay_lsn). The cost: those reads now land on the primary.

notes.text: Stale reads gone even though replicas are still behind
Cost: ~1,100 qps of recent-writer reads moved to primary

feed.text: sorry! switching to 5k batches + pg_sleep while replay_lag > 2s
restart: batch 5000 rows, pause when max(replay_lag) > 2s

beat.hint: WAL now arrives at 15 MB/s while replicas still replay at their 50 MB/s ceiling. The 2.4 GB backlog shrinks by ~35 MB/s, so lag falls steadily. A backfill that watches replay_lag paces itself to what the replicas can absorb.

notes.text: Generation below replay capacity: backlog shrinks
Lag falls ~0.5s per second as the backlog drains

feed.text: primary reads dropped back on their own: replicas pass the LSN check again, so v2.14 stops pinning
done: 42,000,000 rows updated, max replay_lag 1.9s since throttle

beat.hint: Replication lag never goes to zero, it only gets small. Treat replicas as slightly in the past: route a user's reads after their own write by LSN, and pace bulk writes to what replay can absorb.

notes.text: Lag back under 100ms after the backlog drained
Primary reads back to normal: LSN check passes on replicas

report.tldr: A bulk backfill made the primary write WAL faster than replicas could replay it. Lag grew to ~35s, so reads routed to replicas returned rows from before the user's own save.

chain.text: Read after save hits replica: old name

learnings.title: Read your writes from fresh data
learnings.body: After a write, route that user's reads to the primary until a replica's replay LSN passes the commit LSN.

learnings.title: Pace bulk writes to replay
learnings.body: Batch backfills and pause while replay_lag is high; replicas replay WAL in one process.

learnings.title: More replicas ≠ fresher reads
learnings.body: Every replica replays the same WAL at the same speed; scale reads, not freshness.

learnings.title: Alert on lag, not just uptime
learnings.body: Watch pg_stat_replication.replay_lag; a streaming replica can be healthy and 30s behind.

math.title: Why the lag only grows
lines: one replay process     50 MB/s   (a replica applies WAL in a single process)
by the time the fix ships  about 2.4 GB behind, which reads as tens of seconds of lag

myths.truth: Every replica replays the same WAL at the same speed, so another one is just as far behind. It also adds one more stream for the primary to feed.
Replica CPU stayed low. Replay is limited by one process, not by the machine around it.
